newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban warplanes attack Afghan foes.
newsitem.headline: Taleban warplanes attack Afghan foes.

text.p: Taleban warplanes have bombed villages and positions controlled by former Afghan government forces as efforts to forge a ceasefire between the two sides appeared to falter, witnesses said on Friday.

Jet fighters were heard flying low over the capital on Thursday and early on Friday, apparently part of raids on the forces of Ahmad Shah Masood, who has advanced to within rocket range of the capital Kabul in the past week.
A warplane belong to the Taleban bombed the town of Jabal os-Siraj on Friday, the headquarters of Masood, attracting a burst of anti-aircraft fire but causing no casualties, witnesses said.
The plane flew in from behind the Hindu Kush before dropping a bomb into a nearby field. The raid follows a similar sortie on Thursday on the town, 70 km (44 miles) north of Kabul.
At least 14 people died on the same day in an air attack on the village of Kalakan 25 km (15 miles) north of Kabul on the same road.
Masood's forces appeared deadlocked on Friday in their efforts to capture the pass of De Sabz on the easternmost road north of Kabul.

The Taleban, who took the capital four weeks ago, said on Thursday that northern Uzbek chief Abdul Rashid Dostum was now fighting alongside Masood, the Pakistan-based Afghan Islamic Press (AIP) said, quoting acting information minister Amir Khan Mutaqi.
The Taleban had been careful to distinguish between Masood, whom they vowed to crush, and Dostum, with whom they have said they are trying to negotiate.
It was not immediately clear whether Mutaqi's statement marked an end to such efforts.
Both Pakistan and United Nations envoy Norbert Holl have been shuttling between Kabul, Dostum's stronghold of Mazar-i- Sharif and the Taleban headquarters of Kandahar hoping to broker a ceasefire.
Holl was due to fly to Kandahar on Thursday but there was no immediate word on whether his mission had been successful.
Afghan watchers say that it is unlikely that Masood will try to take the city by forces, fearing a bloodbath that would further anger a population weary of war.
But despite occasional shifts in the front line, the two sides do not appear to have the force necessary to break a stalemate on the two roads north of the city.

There was no immediate report on the military situation there on Friday, but the two sides have traded mortar, artillery and rocket fire for the past week without giving or gaining any significant ground along a strip within 30 minutes' drive of Kabul.
